# CS 27.1093 — Induction system icing protection

> [!summary]
> CS 27.1093 requires the induction system of a small rotorcraft to be protected
> against icing. It is a CS-27 specification, not a CS-E one, and the rotorcraft
> applicant owns it. Sub-points (a) and (c) are reciprocating engine provisions
> and differ from the CS-29 text in substance. Sub-point (b) is the turbine
> engine case, and it is word for word the CS-29 one: operation in icing and in
> snow across the flight power range, and a 30-minute ground idle.

## Requirement

The verbs below are CS-27's own. They bind the rotorcraft applicant, not the
engine applicant. See `## Bearing on this engine` for what reaches CS-E.

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **(a)** | Provide means in each reciprocating engine air induction system to prevent and eliminate icing. | Required |
| **(a)** | Unless this is done by other means, show (a)(1) to (a)(4) in air free of visible moisture at a temperature of –1°C (30°F) and with the engines at 75% of maximum continuous power. | Required |
| **(a)(1)** | Each rotorcraft with sea-level engines using conventional venturi carburettors has a preheater that can provide a heat rise of 50°C (90°F). | Required |
| **(a)(2)** | Each rotorcraft with sea-level engines using carburettors tending to prevent icing has a sheltered alternate source of air, and the preheat supplied to the alternate air intake is not less than that provided by the engine cooling air downstream of the cylinders. | Required |
| **(a)(3)** | Each rotorcraft with altitude engines using conventional venturi carburettors has a preheater capable of providing a heat rise of 67°C (120°F). | Required |
| **(a)(4)** | Each rotorcraft with altitude engines using carburettors tending to prevent icing has a preheater that can provide a heat rise of (a)(4)(i) or (a)(4)(ii). | Required |
| **(a)(4)(i)** | 56°C (100°F). | Required |
| **(a)(4)(ii)** | If a fluid de-icing system is used, at least 22°C (40°F). | Relief |
| **(b)(1)** | Show that each turbine engine and its air inlet system can operate throughout the flight power range of the engine, including idling, as set out in (b)(1)(i) and (b)(1)(ii). | Required |
| **(b)(1)(i)** | Operate without accumulating ice on engine or inlet system components that would adversely affect engine operation or cause a serious loss of power, under the icing conditions specified in appendix C of CS-29. | Required |
| **(b)(1)(ii)** | Operate in snow, both falling and blowing, without adverse effect on engine operation, within the limitations established for the rotorcraft. | Required |
| **(b)(2)** | Idle each turbine engine for 30 minutes on the ground, with the air bleed available for engine icing protection at its critical condition, without adverse effect, in an atmosphere that is at a temperature between –9°C and –1°C (15° and 30°F) and has a liquid water content not less than 0.3 grams per cubic metre in the form of drops having a mean effective diameter of not less than 20 microns. Follow the 30 minutes with momentary operation at take-off power or thrust. | Required |
| **(b)(2)** | During the 30 minutes of idle operation, the engine may be run up periodically to a moderate power or thrust setting in a manner acceptable to the Agency. | Permitted |
| **(c)** | For each engine having superchargers to pressurise the air before it enters the carburettor, the heat rise in the air caused by that supercharging at any altitude may be utilised in determining compliance with (a), if the heat rise utilised is that which will be available, automatically, for the applicable altitude and operating condition because of supercharging. | Permitted |

Sub-points (a) and (c) address carburettor icing on a reciprocating engine. They
are recorded because the note records the point whole, not because they reach a
turboshaft. Sub-point (b) carries the whole turbine engine content, and it asks
for a demonstration of operation rather than a heat rise [ext CS 27.1093(b)].

Sub-point (b)(1) does not stand on CS-27 alone. The icing conditions it names
are those of "appendix C of CS-29" [ext CS 27.1093(b)(1)(i)], so a small
rotorcraft is cleared against the large rotorcraft code's icing envelopes.

Sub-point (b)(2) states the ground case entirely in numbers: 30 minutes at idle,
an atmosphere between –9°C and –1°C (15° and 30°F), a liquid water content not
less than 0.3 grams per cubic metre, and drops of a mean effective diameter of
not less than 20 microns [ext CS 27.1093(b)(2)]. The bleed sits at its critical
condition for the whole period, and momentary operation at take-off power closes
the test. The permission that follows is narrow: periodic run-ups to a moderate
power or thrust setting, agreed with the Agency [ext CS 27.1093(b)(2)]. It does
not shorten the 30 minutes.

[VERIFY: unlisted construction. Sub-point (a)(4)(ii) states a lower heat rise,
at least 22°C (40°F), where a fluid de-icing system is used. The phrasing is
declaratory and is neither one of the seven source verbs nor a listed
declaratory form. The row carries Relief, reading the sub-point as an exemption
from the 56°C (100°F) of (a)(4)(i) that the de-icing system earns. The sub-point
is reciprocating engine content and reaches no turboshaft either way.]

### Differences from CS 29.1093

The turbine engine content is the same in both codes, sub-point for sub-point,
and the differences of expression carry no obligation with them. They are listed
in [[CS 29.1093]] and not repeated here.

The reciprocating engine content differs in substance, in three places. CS-27
sets the intro condition of (a) at 75% of maximum continuous power, where CS-29
sets it at 60% [ext CS 29.1093(a)]. For sea-level engines with carburettors
tending to prevent icing, CS-27 asks for a sheltered alternate source of air
whose preheat "is not less than that provided by the engine cooling air
downstream of the cylinders" [ext CS 27.1093(a)(2)], where CS-29 asks instead
for a preheater giving a heat rise of 39°C (70°F) [ext CS 29.1093(a)(2)]. For
altitude engines with such carburettors, CS-27 allows 56°C (100°F) or, where a
fluid de-icing system is used, at least 22°C (40°F), where CS-29 states 56°C
(100°F) alone [ext CS 29.1093(a)(4)]. CS-27 also writes (a)(3) as a preheater
"capable of providing" the heat rise and (c) in terms of superchargers in the
plural; neither changes the duty. None of this reaches a turboshaft.

### Acceptable means

CS-27 carries an AMC to the icing sub-point, AMC1 27.1093(b)(1)(i). It is not
sliced into `work/external/`, so this note carries no AMC material and lists no
accepted means. The same gap exists on the CS-29 side and is recorded in
[[CS 29.1093]].

## Bearing on this engine

CS 27.1093 creates no CS-E obligation. It binds the rotorcraft applicant, and
the article it covers is the aircraft induction system, not the engine type
design. Sub-points (a) and (c) reach no turboshaft, because they are
reciprocating engine provisions [ext CS 27.1093(a)], [ext CS 27.1093(c)].
Sub-point (b) does reach this engine, because the thing tested there is the
turbine engine itself.

**What the rotorcraft applicant must show.** Three demonstrations, all on the
turbine engine. First, that the engine and its air inlet system operate
throughout the flight power range, including idling, without accumulating ice
that would adversely affect engine operation or cause a serious loss of power,
under the icing conditions of appendix C of CS-29 [ext CS 27.1093(b)(1)(i)].
Second, that they operate in falling and blowing snow without adverse effect,
within the limitations established for the rotorcraft
[ext CS 27.1093(b)(1)(ii)]. Third, the 30-minute ground idle at the critical
icing protection bleed condition, closed by momentary operation at take-off
power [ext CS 27.1093(b)(2)].

**The engine evidence they rest on.** [[CS-E 780]] produces it: the engine
applicant must establish that the engine functions satisfactorily in flight and
on the ground throughout the applicable atmospheric icing conditions
[CS-E 780(a)(1)], taking into account the conditions associated with a
representative installation [CS-E 780(c)]. Which conditions those are comes back
from this point, through the aircraft code reference of
[[CS-E 20|CS-E 20(b)]] [CS-E 780(a)(2)]. The bleed data behind the critical
condition of (b)(2) is declared under [[CS-E 690]] and reaches the installer
through the instructions for installing and operating the engine [CS-E 20(d)].
The engine's acceleration to rated Take-off Power, which the closing run-up of
(b)(2) calls on, is demonstrated under [[CS-E 745|CS-E 745(a)(2)]]. The flight
power range itself is bounded by the ratings declared under [[CS-E 40]].

Each of these is the same on both sides of the code question, because the
turbine engine sub-points are identical. [[CS 29.1093]] sets out how the engine
evidence and the airframe demonstration meet, and this note does not repeat it.

What is specific to CS-27 is where the icing envelopes come from. CS-27 has no
icing appendix of its own in this point and borrows CS-29's
[ext CS 27.1093(b)(1)(i)], so an engine cleared for the CS-29 case needs no
further icing envelope for the CS-27 case.

[VERIFY: whether the installation is certificated under CS-27 or CS-29.
[[CS-E 30]] carries the open item. For this point the answer changes nothing the
engine applicant must supply, because the turbine engine sub-points of the two
codes are the same.]
